title: Bones, Bombs, and Break Points: The Geography of Economic Activity
research_question: What explains the spatial distribution of economic activity within a country, particularly the variation and persistence of regional population densities over time? To what extent do temporary but severe destructive shocks to cities permanently alter their relative size, versus being reversed as cities revert to their prior position in the size distribution?
data_description: The study assembles two complementary datasets on Japan. The first is a long-run regional panel covering roughly 8,000 years: counts of 28,013 Jomon-period (−6000 to −300) and 10,530 Yayoi-period (−300 to 300) archaeological sites from Koyama (1978), and regional population from Kito (1996) covering 68 provinces (kuni) for census years 725, 800, 900, 1150, 1600, 1721, 1798, and 1872, plus prefectural censuses for 1920 and 1998. Data are harmonized to 39 comparable regions and expressed as population per square kilometer. The second dataset covers 303 Japanese cities with populations exceeding 30,000 in 1925, with five-year population observations from 1925 to 1965 (1945 census delayed to 1947). City-level wartime variables include deaths and missing per capita, buildings destroyed per capita, percentage of built-up area destroyed (USSBS, 66 cities), and per-capita government reconstruction expenditures.
institutional_context: Japan provides an unusually long, well-documented record of regional population, originating in the Taika tax reforms (646) and implemented from 702, with provincial censuses motivated by feudal taxation. The country's economy passed through dramatic transformations: hunter-gatherer Jomon society, the Yayoi introduction of agriculture and metallurgy, feudal regimes centered successively at Nara, Kyoto, and Tokyo, more than two centuries of self-imposed isolation beginning in the 1630s, the Meiji-era reopening to trade and industrialization from the 1870s, and full modern industrialization by the late twentieth century. The setting also includes the Allied strategic bombing campaign of World War II, which targeted 66 cities, destroyed roughly half of urban structures and two-thirds of productive capacity, killed about 300,000 people, and included the firebombing of Tokyo and the nuclear attacks on Hiroshima and Nagasaki—an unusually large, variable, and clearly temporary destruction of urban capital.
